semantics.note: A firm necessity claim: reliable reasoning about time and prices needs a proper model. The 'without a proper model' qualifier is kept. The 'might... only superficially' clause is a concession, not a hedge on the main claim.

contract.note: The contract fairly says 'proper model', 'reliably' and 'superficially' are undefined. Whether LLMs have world models is itself disputed, so no system can be placed on either side of the line, and the claim cannot be tested.

reviews.rationale: The claim is firm but untestable. 'Proper model' has no definition, and 'reliably' and 'superficially' have no threshold. The sources considered measure temporal reasoning but don't sort systems by whether they have a world model. There are no evidence items, so nothing can be scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Captures the core claim: LLM agents have security and reliability problems. The 'increasingly' trend is dropped, but the contract says so openly and the source wording is garbled.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: documented security vulnerabilities and reliability failures in LLM agents before the post. The 2025 target period is reasonable. Leaving the trend untested doesn't stretch the claim either way.

evidence.note: A company disclosure from July 2025. OpenAI calls prompt injection a risk for agentic systems generally. That is an admission of a known vulnerability class, not an independent finding, but it fits the security part.
A July 2025 news report of a Replit agent deleting a live database during a code freeze. The sidebar links in the snapshot are later material and were not used.
A May 2025 benchmark preprint: the best agent completed only 30% of realistic workplace tasks on its own. It measures limited reliability in the period.

reviews.rationale: Sources from the target period document both a security vulnerability class (prompt injection, which OpenAI acknowledges) and reliability failures (the Replit incident, the 30% completion rate). The packet lists no counterevidence. Whether the problems were increasing was not tested.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Preprosterous to think it is going to' expresses firm expectation, conditional on failing to induce chess rules. The 'just from big data' scope is kept, though it is listed as an antecedent rather than a scope condition.

contract.note: The contract fairly notes that no system is named, 'robust' is undefined, and 'all it needs to know' has no threshold. The antecedent's status is unknown, so the claim cannot be scored.

reviews.rationale: A conditional forecast with no deadline whose antecedent is unknown: no named system has been shown to lack a robust chess-rules model. The consequent also has no measure. Under policy, a conditional whose antecedent is unknown is not scored. There are no evidence items.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A faithful paraphrase of a comparative generalisation with no metric. In context it works largely as a rhetorical warning about trusting LLMs.

contract.note: The contract rightly says there is no common metric for comparing 'saying' with 'doing', and no task domain. Testing it would need an interpretation the speaker didn't supply.

reviews.rationale: The comparison has no measure, domain or shared scale, so it can't be tested as stated. The sources considered study the gap between an LLM's own words and its own actions, not imitation of human speech versus human action. Not adjudicable.
